questions.q: What does PPO replace TRPO's hard KL-divergence constraint with?
options: A second, separate neural network
Clipping the probability ratio so it cannot stray too far from 1
A larger replay buffer
A fixed learning rate schedule
questions.explain: PPO approximates TRPO's trust-region effect by simply clipping the probability ratio between new and old policy, avoiding the need for conjugate gradients or KL-constrained optimization.

questions.q: Why can PPO safely reuse the same collected rollout for multiple epochs of gradient updates?
options: Because the environment resets between every epoch
Because the clipping mechanism keeps repeated updates from drifting too far from the policy that generated the data
Because PPO does not use advantage estimates
Because multiple epochs are mathematically identical to one epoch
questions.explain: Clipping bounds how much the policy can change relative to the data-generating policy, which is what makes it safe to extract several gradient updates from one on-policy rollout.

questions.q: In the PPO training loop, what happens to a rollout after it has been used for updates?
options: It is stored permanently and reused forever
It is discarded, since it was collected on-policy under the pre-update policy, and a fresh rollout is collected with the updated policy
It is averaged with all previous rollouts
It is sent to a separate target network
questions.explain: Because PPO's data is on-policy, once the policy has been updated the old rollout no longer reflects the current policy, so it's discarded and new data is collected.

questions.q: In the Stable-Baselines3 PPO example, what does the clip_range parameter correspond to?
options: The discount factor gamma
The epsilon in the clipped surrogate objective that bounds the probability ratio
The number of parallel environments
The replay buffer capacity
questions.explain: clip_range sets epsilon, the parameter that defines how far the probability ratio is allowed to move from 1 before being clipped, covered in full in the next lesson.

questions.q: Why did PPO become the dominant algorithm for RLHF specifically?
options: Because it requires no reward model at all
Because its clipping mechanism makes it robust to noisy, expensive-to-evaluate reward signals without catastrophically derailing the model from one bad batch
Because it was the first RL algorithm ever invented
Because it eliminates the need for a policy network
questions.explain: PPO's bounded updates make it well-suited to the noisy reward signals produced by a learned reward model scoring LLM outputs, preventing a single bad batch from destabilizing a large pretrained model.
